dailyBrief.text: Tough morning, Cleveland: the Guardians' season ended last night in St. Petersburg, a 7-3 loss to Tampa Bay in ALCS Game 6 that sends the Rays to the World Series instead. Overnight, Zelenskiy arrived in Oslo for talks with U.S. envoy Witkoff and European leaders on ending the war, even as a Russian drone killed three people on the highway south of Kyiv. Closer to home, Nestlé confirmed it will close its Solon factory by the end of 2027 and move production to South Carolina — the campus stays, and the city is promising job help for affected workers. Solon woke up clear and cold at 37°, but it's a sunny, dry day ahead with a high near 68°. Today in town: the CLEO on the Go Luncheon at Mavis Public House at 11:30, and the Browns get a quiet week to enjoy first place before Sunday at Tennessee.

weekBrief.text: It's a crisp, dry fall week in Solon: sunny skies almost every day, highs in the mid-to-upper 60s and chilly nights in the 30s and 40s, with today topping out near 68°. The Guardians' October run is over after Monday's Game 6 loss, so the sports baton passes on: the Cavs open Thursday night at Philadelphia and play their home opener Saturday against Brooklyn, and the first-place Browns head to Tennessee on Sunday. Around town it's a full week — trunk-or-treat Thursday in Solon, Heinen's clam bake Friday in Chagrin Falls, and Barack Obama rallying in Cleveland on Saturday for the fall races, while Solon digests the news that Nestlé will wind down its factory here by the end of 2027. Grocery play of the week is still Giant Eagle's free-turkey deal — spend $350 by November 8 — and with the baby countdown very much on, it's a good week to knock a few more checklist items off together.

Zelenskiy calls Oslo talks a step forward as Witkoff prepares to take a peace document to Moscow
items.summary:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said Tuesday he heard encouraging signs from the American side after a summit in Oslo with U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff and European leaders, and after a morning phone call with Secretary of State Marco Rubio. President Trump added his own pressure, saying it is time to reach a deal to end a war now in its fifth year.

The Oslo meeting brought together Norway's prime minister, Finland's president, European and NATO officials, and Witkoff in person, with fellow envoy Jared Kushner joining remotely while ill. Zelenskiy said the group aligned on a framework covering a peace settlement, security guarantees for Ukraine, a wider European security arrangement that could include a path toward EU membership, and post-war recovery financing. He said he was assured those guarantees would be strong, and that Ukraine brought new proposals of its own to the table.

The stakes now shift to Moscow. Witkoff is expected to carry the agreed document to Russian negotiators on Wednesday, which makes the next 24 hours the first real test of whether the Oslo alignment survives contact with the Kremlin. Zelenskiy also used the day to press practical needs — ballistic missile interceptors, early warning of Russian launches, and full restoration of the Starlink links his forces depend on — and even floated that the time may have come for a three-way meeting of leaders.

Watch Wednesday's Moscow presentation and any Kremlin response. A concrete Russian counter-proposal would mark real movement; silence or new conditions would suggest Oslo produced alignment among allies, but not yet a negotiation.

items.title: Alberta votes decisively to stay in Canada, and markets cheer the certainty
items.summary:
Alberta voters have overwhelmingly chosen to remain part of Canada. In Monday's referendum, about 76.5 percent voted to stay, against roughly 23.4 percent who wanted to begin a legal process that could eventually have led to a binding vote on independence, with official results due October 29.

Premier Danielle Smith called the vote under pressure from separatists inside her own United Conservative Party, even though she personally backed staying. Prime Minister Mark Carney campaigned in the province in the final days, warning that a vote against Canada would bring years of uncertainty, and pointing to his own gestures toward the oil industry, including support for a new Pacific pipeline. On Tuesday the Canadian dollar strengthened to a four-week high, with traders calling the result the least disruptive outcome possible.

The result is a significant win for Carney's unity agenda at a moment of trade conflict with the United States, and it pushes separatism back to the margins for now. It does not erase the grievances behind the vote — a long-running sense in Alberta that Ottawa takes the province's oil wealth while giving it little say, a complaint with roots stretching back decades.

Separatist leaders have vowed to keep organizing, and the tension inside Smith's party remains unresolved. Watch her evening address to the province and whether the issue resurfaces inside the UCP.

items.title: Romania finally has a full government as parliament confirms a new prime minister
items.summary:
Romania's parliament on Tuesday confirmed independent Luca Niculescu as prime minister, ending nearly six months without a fully empowered government. Niculescu won the confidence vote with 280 votes, well above the 233 he needed.

A 55-year-old former journalist who later served as a diplomat and deputy foreign minister, Niculescu was nominated by centrist President Nicusor Dan. It was Dan's fourth attempt to install a government since the previous broad pro-European coalition collapsed in early May. Niculescu will lead a minority government made up of leftists and technocrats, and told lawmakers he was not asking for a blank check, only for a government with full powers after months of crisis.

The long stalemate has weighed on investor confidence and put pressure on Romania's investment-grade credit rating. The new government's job is a hard one: shrink one of the European Union's largest budget deficits, support an economy that is contracting, scrap an extra turnover tax on companies, and find room to raise pensions that have been frozen for two years.

Analysts warn the minority government could be short-lived given the size of that repair job in a NATO and EU member state on the alliance's eastern flank.

items.title: Malaysia cancels the registration of its main opposition coalition ahead of elections
items.summary:
Malaysia's Registrar of Societies on Tuesday cancelled the registration of Perikatan Nasional, the country's main opposition coalition, after a bitter dispute between its two largest parties. The decision means the coalition's member parties cannot contest upcoming elections under a shared banner.

The fight pits PAS, the conservative Islamist party that holds more seats than any other single party in the 222-member parliament, against Bersatu, led by former prime minister Muhyiddin Yassin. Bersatu had complained it was shut out of a coalition council meeting in July, calling it a breach of the coalition's constitution. The registrar said the coalition's response to a warning last month failed to refute the grounds for cancellation.

The timing matters. A state vote in Malacca is due November 14, in the latest test for Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim after defeats in two other regional polls this year, and tensions inside his own ruling coalition could also trigger an early general election.

The coalition's secretary-general called the move an attempt to weaken opponents ahead of the Malacca election and said it would file a legal challenge. Watch whether the courts restore the registration before campaigning begins in earnest.

items.title: Israel's central bank is expected to pause rate cuts a week before the election
items.summary:
The Bank of Israel is expected to keep its benchmark interest rate at a four-year low of 3.25 percent on Wednesday, pausing after three straight cuts, according to a Reuters poll in which all 15 economists surveyed forecast a hold.

The easing cycle began last November and has delivered five quarter-point cuts as inflation settled inside the government's 1 to 3 percent target range, most recently edging up to 1.6 percent in September. The economy also bounced back sharply in the second quarter, growing at a 15.4 percent annualized rate, even as the shekel weakened to a nine-month low against the dollar.

Politics hangs over the decision. A cut this week could be seen as helping Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ahead of the October 27 election, and polls show neither his bloc nor the main opposition grouping on course for a majority. Analysts cited by Reuters said political uncertainty argues for the central bank to wait, with at least one more cut to 3 percent still widely expected later.

The decision lands Wednesday at 4 p.m. local time, less than a week before Israelis vote.

items.title: Beijing blasts the U.S. DeepSeek ban, saying it ignores the two leaders' consensus
items.summary:
China's commerce ministry on Tuesday sharply criticized a U.S. order removing the Chinese AI model DeepSeek from federal civilian government systems, saying the move harms Chinese companies and disregards understandings reached by the two countries' leaders.

The U.S. Department of Homeland Security ordered DeepSeek products, and third-party services built on its models, stripped from civilian agency IT systems, and barred agencies from buying them in the future. DHS said the models pose multiple threat vectors and warned that their use by government employees or vendors could transfer sensitive data to China.

Beijing said it is strongly dissatisfied and firmly opposed, urged Washington to revoke what it called discriminatory measures, and said it would take all necessary measures to safeguard its interests. It also pointed to the AI dialogue mechanism the two sides have set up as the proper channel for disputes like this.

The exchange is a reminder that AI has become a front-line trade and security issue between the two powers. Watch for any Chinese countermeasure aimed at U.S. tech firms, and for whether the dialogue channel is actually used.

items.title: House Republicans quietly scale back hopes for a big redistricting boost
items.summary:
House Republicans are quietly lowering expectations for the nationwide redistricting push they expected to reshape the midterm map, Axios reports. Strategists who once talked about a double-digit gain now privately worry the whole effort could net the party as little as one seat nationally.

Early this summer Republicans believed new maps had created 16 more GOP-friendly seats — five in Texas, four in Florida, two in Ohio, and one each in Alabama, Louisiana, Missouri, North Carolina and Tennessee. Since then a court tossed the Missouri map, Democrats have opened an eight-point lead in national Washington Post-ABC polling, and California's counter-map, engineered by Governor Gavin Newsom, is expected to deliver Democrats five seats of their own. In a worst case for the GOP, the two parties' gains nearly cancel out.

The biggest shift is among Latino voters. GOP support has eroded sharply with a group President Trump nearly won outright in 2024, putting supposedly safe new seats in Texas and Florida in doubt. House Republican campaign chief Tom Emmer conceded he would be surprised if the party won all five Texas seats and shocked if it won all four in Florida.

With early voting rolling toward the November 3 midterms, the map fight looks less like a Republican lock and more like a wash — which puts even more weight on turnout and candidate quality in a handful of districts.

items.title: Hegseth's quiet Netanyahu meeting fuels talk of a renewed U.S. push against Iran
items.summary:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth traveled to Israel without announcement on Monday and met Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu at Ovda Air Base in the south of the country, where American fighter jets and refueling aircraft are deployed, according to Axios reporting cited by the Daily Caller.

The meeting came eight days before Israel's parliamentary election and about two weeks before the U.S. midterms, amid discussions between Washington and Jerusalem about potentially resuming large-scale military operations against Iran. The Pentagon pointed reporters to Hegseth's social media post about visiting U.S. service members in the Central Command area, and neither the Pentagon nor Israel's embassy in Washington commented on the substance of the talks. One senior military official quoted in the report suggested operations against Iran could soon intensify.

The visit also landed in the middle of a split inside the administration's public posture: President Trump has given Netanyahu his complete endorsement for next week's election, while Vice President JD Vance pointedly declined to endorse, saying he is focused on the U.S. midterms.

Watch for any announcement on U.S. force posture in the region, and for how the Iran question plays in both countries' final campaign weeks.

items.title: The federal deficit hit $2 trillion, the largest since the pandemic climb-out
items.summary:
The U.S. budget deficit has reached $2 trillion this fiscal year, according to the latest figures reported by Axios — the largest shortfall since 2021, when the country was climbing out of the pandemic recession.

A major driver is the cost of servicing the national debt at a moment when interest rates are rising, in part because of the inflationary impact of the war with Iran. Higher rates make every dollar of existing debt more expensive to carry, which in turn adds to the borrowing the Treasury has to do — a feedback loop budget watchers have warned about for years.

The number lands two weeks before the midterms, handing both parties a talking point: critics of the administration will cite it as evidence of lost fiscal control, while the White House is likely to argue that growth and tariff revenue will bend the curve over time.

Watch the Treasury's next refunding announcement and any reaction from the bond market, where the 10-year yield has been hovering above 5 percent.

items.title: Supreme Court won't revive the 9/11 plea deal, leaving a 2028 death-penalty trial as the path
items.summary:
The Supreme Court has declined to revive plea agreements for Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, the accused mastermind of the September 11 attacks, and two alleged accomplices — agreements that would have spared them the death penalty in exchange for guilty pleas.

The deals were struck in 2024 and accepted by the official overseeing the Guantanamo war tribunal, then revoked within days by then-Defense Secretary Lloyd Austin after criticism from Republican lawmakers. Military judges initially said Austin lacked the authority to withdraw them; a federal appeals court disagreed, and the justices, in an unsigned order with Justice Kavanaugh not participating, let that ruling stand.

The road ahead is still difficult for prosecutors. A military judge set a trial date of June 2028, but in August threw out Mohammed's confession to FBI agents, ruling it was not given voluntarily — a decision that removes what prosecutors had called the centerpiece of their case. The defendants were captured in 2003, held in secret CIA prisons, and formally charged in 2008, and the case has been delayed for years by fights over interrogation evidence.

For victims' families, who are divided between wanting a full trial and wanting the certainty of a plea, the ruling means the quarter-century-old case will grind on toward a capital trial.

items.title: Trump accuses Omar and Walz of Minnesota fraud as he launches a whistleblower program
items.summary:
President Trump on Tuesday accused Representative Ilhan Omar and Minnesota Governor Tim Walz of being, in his words, 100 percent guilty of facilitating widespread benefit fraud in Minnesota, as his administration rolled out a new whistleblower program encouraging the public to report alleged fraud.

Speaking at an Oval Office event with Dr. Mehmet Oz, FTC Chair Andrew Ferguson, Vice President Vance and online influencer Nick Shirley, Trump also repeated claims about Omar's personal history and suggested she could face jail. Omar has denied committing immigration fraud and says she became a citizen through her father, who was naturalized in 2000. Her Washington home was raided last week by Homeland Security agents, who left with boxes marked as evidence, according to the report.

The accusations arrive two weeks before the midterms and escalate a Minnesota fraud controversy that has become a national political weapon. No charges against Omar or Walz were announced at the event, and the president's claims remain allegations rather than findings by a court or investigator.

Watch for whether the whistleblower program produces formal referrals, and for responses from Omar and Walz, who have disputed the administration's characterizations.

items.title: Dow jumps more than 500 points as money rotates out of tech and into health care
items.summary:
Wall Street closed mixed on Tuesday, but the mix favored the old economy. The Dow rose 1.02 percent to 52,495.88, the S&P 500 added 0.28 percent to 7,712.57, and the Nasdaq eased 0.02 percent, as health care and small caps led and megacap tech wobbled under renewed anxiety about AI spending.

Soft housing data helped the rotation. Pending home sales dropped 7.3 percent from the prior month, Treasury prices rallied, and the Russell 2000 jumped about 1.7 percent while the Nasdaq-100 slipped. A Wall Street Journal report that Anthropic's draft IPO filing shows an $80.7 billion net loss for the first half of 2026 revived questions about whether AI capital spending is producing returns, weighing on Alphabet in particular. Customer-engagement software maker Braze was the day's standout, surging about 52 percent on its Salesforce takeover deal before analysts began cautioning that the move had stretched its valuation.

The session captured the market's split personality two weeks before the midterms: investors are happy to own earnings and cash flow, and increasingly skeptical of open-ended AI build-outs funded with debt.

Wednesday brings Meta and Tesla earnings after the close, plus UK inflation data — the next test of whether the rotation out of tech continues.

items.title: Netflix beats on earnings but guides weak, and the stock slides after hours
items.summary:
Netflix reported third-quarter earnings that beat expectations on Tuesday, then promptly fell nearly 7 percent in after-hours trading after issuing a fourth-quarter profit forecast below what Wall Street wanted.

Third-quarter revenue rose 11.8 percent — the slowest growth rate in nearly three years — and earnings came in at 87 cents a share against an 82-cent average forecast. For the fourth quarter, Netflix forecast net income of $2.79 billion and earnings of 67 cents a share, below analyst expectations of $3.07 billion and 73 cents. The company also trimmed its 2026 advertising revenue forecast to about $2.7 billion from roughly $3 billion, saying some ad products rolled out more slowly than expected.

The report lands days after Netflix laid off about 6 percent of its workforce and replaced two top programming executives, and it reflects a streamer fighting for attention against YouTube and TikTok as much as against rival subscriptions. Netflix said it will lean on licensing more third-party content alongside originals, live events, games and podcasts.

The question for investors is where the next leg of growth comes from. Watch subscriber and engagement commentary, and whether the after-hours slide holds when Meta and Tesla report Wednesday.

items.title: SpaceX posts its first big profit as a public company, powered by its AI segment
items.summary:
SpaceX blew past expectations in its second earnings report as a public company, posting third-quarter revenue of $14.6 billion — up about 161 percent from a year earlier — and net income of $4.4 billion, reversing a $1.1 billion loss in the same quarter last year.

The surprise is what drove it. The company's Super Intelligence segment, its AI business, produced $7.6 billion of revenue, up from $813 million a year ago, making it the largest segment for the first time on the back of cloud services deals, the Cursor acquisition and rising use of its Grok models. Starlink, in the Connectivity segment, brought in about $5.25 billion with 13.6 million subscribers, and the Space segment added about $1.77 billion. Adjusted earnings of roughly 35 cents a share were more than double the consensus estimate, and the stock rose after hours.

The spending matches the ambition: capital expenditures nearly tripled to $19.6 billion in the quarter, with $16.4 billion going into Super Intelligence infrastructure. That burn rate is exactly what skeptics question, even on a blowout quarter.

Management offered no numeric guidance in the release, promising detail on its webcast. Watch whether the AI segment's contracted revenue keeps converting at this pace — that is the bull case, and now the number to beat.

items.title: GM's profit more than doubles and it adds a $20 billion buyback, but the stock still falls
items.summary:
General Motors reported a much stronger third quarter on Tuesday — net income of $3.34 billion, up from $1.33 billion a year earlier, adjusted earnings of $3.70 a share, and revenue of $50 billion — and approved a new $20 billion share buyback. Investors sold the stock anyway, sending it down roughly 7 percent.

The problem was the outlook. GM raised the low end of its full-year profit range but cut the high end, narrowing adjusted EBIT guidance to $14.5 to $15.5 billion from $14 to $16 billion. Unit sales fell 5.5 percent in the quarter on discontinued models, softer EV demand and buyers trading down from large SUVs as fuel prices bite, and the company flagged about $2 billion of commodity inflation along with tariff costs expected near the low end of a $2.5 to $3.5 billion range.

GM is leaning into what makes money — trucks and SUVs, with new Silverado and Sierra pickups coming — and returning cash, having already cut its share count from 904 million to 849 million this year. The market's message was that buybacks cannot substitute for volume growth.

Watch U.S. sales trends into year-end and whether GM's hybrid rethink produces a credible answer for buyers priced out of big trucks.

items.title: Salesforce agrees to buy Braze for $5.66 billion in an AI marketing push
items.summary:
Salesforce has signed a deal to acquire customer-engagement platform Braze for about $5.66 billion including debt, the companies announced Tuesday. Braze shareholders will receive $47.50 in cash per share — a premium of roughly 58 percent over Monday's close — and Braze's stock surged more than 50 percent on the news.

Braze helps marketers respond to live customer behavior in real time, coordinating personalized messages across apps, websites, email, text and WhatsApp for nearly 2,800 customers including Canva, Dairy Queen and Equinox. Salesforce plans to fold the technology into its Marketing Cloud, data platform and AI agent offerings, arguing that knowing the customer at the right moment is where marketing value now sits. Notably, the $47.50 price is still well below the $65 a share at which Braze went public in 2021.

The deal is expected to close in Salesforce's fiscal 2028, subject to shareholder and regulatory approval, and Salesforce said it does not change its fiscal 2027 outlook.

For Salesforce investors, the test is whether Braze revives growth in a marketing cloud that analysts have called in need of new energy. Braze's own shareholders vote next.

items.title: In Asia, the AI trade wobbles again: a Seoul data-center debut flops and chips slide
items.summary:
The AI infrastructure trade took another hit on Tuesday, this time starting in Asia. South Korean AI cloud firm Elice plunged roughly 30 percent in its market debut despite heavy retail demand for the offering, dragging down Korea's Kospi by more than 3.5 percent and pressuring chip names including SK Hynix.

The weakness crossed the Pacific. In U.S. pre-market and early trading, Micron, SanDisk, Intel and Qualcomm all fell, and CoreWeave — which lost more than 25 percent last week on worries about the debt funding its data-center build-out — slid again. The Philadelphia semiconductor index dropped, a day after chip stocks had snapped a long losing streak.

The pattern is becoming familiar: investors are no longer paying any price for AI capacity. Offerings and earnings that once would have been cheered are being interrogated for leverage, utilization and the distance between spending announcements and actual revenue.

Watch CoreWeave and the broader chip index this week, and whether Meta's capital spending guidance on Wednesday calms or confirms the skeptics.

items.title: U.S. men finish sixth at gymnastics worlds — their worst result since 2006 — and miss an Olympic berth
items.summary:
The U.S. men's gymnastics team finished sixth in the team final at the world championships on Tuesday, scoring 245.161 and leaving without the Olympic berth that was on the line. It was the program's worst finish at a world championships since 2006, when the team failed to reach the final at all.

Japan, the reigning world and Olympic champion, won gold again with 251.928, ahead of Russia — competing with a full team at worlds for the first time since 2019 — and China. The American day unraveled in pieces: a fall on pommel horse, a costly high bar routine, and not enough difficulty to absorb the mistakes. The bright spot was specialist Patrick Hoopes, whose 14.833 on pommel horse was the highest U.S. score on any apparatus.

Missing a team Olympic berth at worlds forces the program onto a harder qualification path and raises hard questions about depth behind its top names, two years into an Olympic cycle the U.S. expected to contend in.

Watch for USA Gymnastics' response and the remaining qualification routes — the individual apparatus pathway now matters a great deal more than it did this morning.

items.title: Compounded GLP-1 injections recalled nationwide over possible contamination
items.summary:
A nationwide recall covers compounded tirzepatide injections from Apothecary Pharma over possible contamination, according to the Food and Drug Administration. The recall involves 22 vials of an 18 mg/mL solution in 4-milliliter multidose vials, sold by prescription only, across lots with beyond-use dates running from early October into late November 2026.

Compounded versions of GLP-1 drugs like tirzepatide and semaglutide expanded rapidly while the branded drugs were on the federal shortage list. That permission narrowed once the shortages ended in late 2024 and early 2025, and regulators have been scrutinizing compounders since. The FDA sent Apothecary Pharma a warning letter in December 2025 citing serious deficiencies in how it produces drugs that are supposed to be sterile, saying those deficiencies put patients at risk.

Anyone holding a vial should check the lot number and beyond-use date printed on it against the FDA list before using it. The affected lots run from AP-202622 through AP-202644.

The recall is the latest sign that the compounded GLP-1 market, which millions turned to when branded drugs were scarce or expensive, is entering a stricter era. Watch for further FDA enforcement against other compounders.

items.title: U.S. orders DeepSeek removed from most civilian government systems, and bans buying it
items.summary:
The Department of Homeland Security has ordered DeepSeek products — and third-party services built on the Chinese AI model — removed from U.S. civilian government IT systems, and barred agencies from acquiring them in the future, according to a notice published this week.

DHS said the models pose multiple threat vectors, warning that use by government employees or vendors could transfer sensitive data to China, and that the models themselves may contain malware or other security vulnerabilities. The order, signed in July and made public Monday, was issued under the Federal Acquisition Supply Chain Security Act after a recommendation from the interagency Federal Acquisition Security Council. It reaches beyond the DeepSeek app itself to cover tools developed using DeepSeek implementations, which makes compliance a supply-chain hunt for agencies and their vendors.

Private individuals and companies in the U.S. can still use DeepSeek legally. The ban covers federal civilian agencies — Treasury, State and Justice among them — while defense and intelligence systems fall under separate authorities.

Beijing has already condemned the order as discriminatory. Watch how quickly vendors disclose DeepSeek-derived components in their government products; that disclosure process is where the order will bite hardest.

items.title: Housing stays stuck: pending sales fall, starts slip, and high mortgage rates do the damage
items.summary:
Fresh housing data on Tuesday painted the same picture the market has seen for months: activity is being suppressed by high mortgage rates, even though prices are holding up because so few distressed properties are coming to market.

Pending home sales fell sharply — down 7.3 percent from the prior month in one widely followed read, and 11.3 percent below a year earlier — while building permits were down about 3 percent year over year, housing starts down about 7.4 percent, and completions down about 14 percent. With the 10-year Treasury yield above 5 percent, mortgage costs remain near levels that lock existing owners into their current loans and price many first-time buyers out entirely.

The soft data had one market upside: it pulled Treasury yields slightly lower on the day and helped fuel the rotation into smaller, rate-sensitive stocks.

The Federal Reserve's path is the swing factor. A Reuters poll of economists expects a hold at next week's meeting with a possible hike in December — a combination that offers homebuyers little relief before spring.

items.title: An unconfirmed Iran peace proposal whipsawed oil and stocks in the middle of the day
items.summary:
U.S. stocks staged a midday reversal on Tuesday after reports of an unconfirmed Qatar-Pakistan peace proposal on the Iran war sent oil prices retreating from their highs and healthcare shares surging — a reminder of how completely the Middle East now drives the trading day.

Oil had traded at its highest levels since April earlier in the session, with Brent above $110 at one point, on fears tied to the Iran war and attacks on Saudi infrastructure. When the peace-proposal reports crossed, crude pulled back and the Dow pushed to a gain of more than 1 percent, even as the AI infrastructure trade continued to unravel in the background.

Nothing about the proposal has been confirmed by Washington, Tehran or the mediators, and similar reports have moved markets before without producing an agreement. The conflicting signals out of the region — including separate reporting suggesting U.S. operations could intensify — left traders pricing headlines rather than facts by the close.

Treat the proposal as unverified until a government confirms it. If it is real, expect oil to give back much more of its war premium; if it evaporates, Tuesday's reversal likely does too.

items.title: Nestlé will close its Solon factory by the end of 2027 — the campus, and its research jobs, stay
items.summary:
Nestlé plans to close its Solon factory by the end of 2027, ending nearly six decades of manufacturing at a site that traces back to Stouffer's. Production of frozen meal pouches for the company's food-service business will move gradually to its existing plant in Gaffney, South Carolina, with Solon production expected to end in the third quarter of 2027 and the factory closing in the final quarter.

Employees learned the news Monday. Hundreds of positions are expected to be affected, though Nestlé has not confirmed an exact number; a formal WARN notice is expected around March 2027. The company says affected workers will get separation benefits and transition help, and can apply for other openings in Ohio. Its Streetsboro distribution center and West 25th Street factory in Cleveland are unaffected, and the broader Solon campus — research, development and corporate operations — remains open. The city lists Nestlé Prepared Foods as Solon's second-largest employer, at roughly 2,314 full-time-equivalent positions across its local operations, which is why the decision reaches well beyond the factory floor.

Mayor Edward Kraus called it difficult news for Solon families and said the city will work with Nestlé and state and regional partners on job placement and support, while noting the research and corporate presence the city keeps. The factory had already seen cuts in recent years, including 216 positions announced in 2024.

The long runway matters: with production running into late 2027, affected workers and the city have time — but the test will be whether the promised transition help turns into comparable local jobs.

items.title: Browns shuffle the practice squad with six moves on Tuesday
items.summary:
The first-place Browns made six practice squad moves on Tuesday, signing offensive tackle Andrew Coker, punter Wes Pahl and safety John Saunders, while releasing tight end Devin Culp and defensive tackle Chris Williams and placing receiver Bub Means on the practice squad injured list with a knee injury.

The Williams release is the read-between-the-lines move: Cleveland's defensive interior has been thinned by injuries, and letting a tackle go can signal that help is getting healthier. Maliek Collins handled a heavy snap load against Baltimore and the remaining group held the Ravens scoreless over their final nine drives in Sunday's 13-10 win, which moved the Browns to 4-2 and alone atop the AFC North.

None of Tuesday's signings has appeared in a regular-season NFL game for Cleveland, and Coker — an undrafted tackle out of TCU who has bounced through the Raiders' and Bengals' practice squads — is depth insurance rather than a Sunday answer.

The real injury news will come from the practice field this week. Watch Mason Graham's participation and whether Mike Hall gets back to work ahead of Sunday's trip to Tennessee.

items.title: Shedeur Sanders signs with a new agency as trade rumors swirl around the Browns' backup
items.summary:
Shedeur Sanders has signed with a new agency for representation, a personal move that has intensified trade speculation around the Browns' young quarterback as the November 10 deadline approaches.

Sanders has watched from the sideline while Deshaun Watson, returning from the Achilles injury that cost him the entire 2025 season, has solidified the starting job through six games. Watson's raw numbers against Baltimore were modest — 16 of 26 for 164 yards and no touchdowns — but he delivered the late 33-yard strike to Jerry Jeudy that set up the winning score, and the Browns are 4-2 and in first place, which makes a quarterback controversy a hard sell inside the building.

New representation does not mean a trade is coming, and winning teams rarely subtract from the quarterback room mid-season. But a player with Sanders' profile, limited snaps and clear ambition is exactly the kind of name that circulates when contenders and quarterback-needy teams start calling.

Watch the deadline chatter over the next three weeks — and whether the Browns give Sanders any designed snaps to either showcase or develop him.

items.title: 'I hope this isn't the last time I put a Cleveland jersey on': Hedges faces free agency
items.summary:
A day after the Guardians' season ended with a 7-3 loss to Tampa Bay in Game 6 of the ALCS, veteran catcher Austin Hedges made his wishes plain: he wants to come back to Cleveland.

Hedges, 34, is headed for free agency after appearing in 78 regular-season games and hitting .247 with six home runs and 25 RBIs. His value has never been mainly about the bat — it is his handling of a pitching staff, his clubhouse presence, and the trust the organization places in him in October, when the Guardians leaned on his experience through a run that ended two wins short of the World Series. Cleveland finished 85-77, won the AL Central, and fell to the Rays four games to two.

The front office now faces the usual winter math: a beloved veteran catcher at a price that makes sense, against younger options already in the system. Hedges' comments give Cleveland the first word if it wants it — players who want to be here, at the right number, tend to stay.

Watch the early weeks of free agency. If the Guardians move quickly, it signals they see Hedges as part of the 2027 bridge; if they wait, the market may decide for them.

items.title: Federal judge extends Cleveland's police consent decree through 2028
items.summary:
A federal judge has extended Cleveland's police consent decree for two more years, keeping the Cleveland Division of Police under independent federal monitoring until at least October 13, 2028.

In his ruling, U.S. District Senior Judge Solomon Oliver Jr. applauded the city for its continued efforts toward compliance, while noting that areas of the decree remain unmet. The monitoring team's latest assessment of the department found substantial and effective compliance in three areas, operational compliance in five, partial compliance in three, and non-compliance in one. The extension follows the judge's earlier refusal to end the decree after the city and the Justice Department jointly asked to terminate it, a request he called premature.

The decree, in place since 2015 after a Justice Department investigation found a pattern of excessive force, was meant to be a framework for systemic change rather than a checklist. Whether Cleveland can sustain reforms without a federal monitor remains the unresolved question hanging over the case.

Watch the city's appeal and the monitor's next assessment cycle — the compliance grades, especially the single non-compliance area, will decide whether 2028 is the real end date.

items.title: Monken backs Jerry Jeudy as trade talk floats around the Browns' quietest receiver
items.summary:
Head coach Todd Monken offered pointed support for Jerry Jeudy this week, praising how the receiver carries his practice work into games — comments that read as a signal while Jeudy's name floats in trade speculation ahead of the November 10 deadline.

The production case against Jeudy is real: 12 catches for 150 yards through six games, an average of 25 yards a game, putting him on pace for the lowest yardage total of his career two years after a 1,229-yard Pro Bowl season in Cleveland. He has become the third option in a run-first, defense-led offense.

The counter-case is timing. Jeudy has produced in two of the Browns' biggest fourth quarters this season, including the 33-yard catch that set up Sunday's winner against Baltimore. A 4-2 team in first place does not usually trade away the receiver its quarterback trusts most when a game is on the line — and Monken's comments suggest the coaching staff sees value the box score misses.

The next couple of games before the deadline will tell. A bigger role keeps Jeudy in Cleveland; continued silence in the offense makes the rumors louder.
